#4675. Giving Thanks for Sexual Options—That Many Don’t Use

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Sad but true: Many of our sexual rights have been eroded in the last 10 years. School sex education is the least accurate and most harmful it’s been in decades. Restrictions on adult entertainment and reproductive rights, as well as the coercion of physicians' and psychologists' speech, are getting increasingly onerous.

That said, let’s be thankful for the sexual freedoms, technologies, and options we do have right now. Here are some that many people don’t take full advantage of—and I encourage you to do so.

The morning-after pill prevents pregnancy by preventing or delaying ovulation. If you don’t ovulate, you can’t get pregnant.

The morning-after pill will not end a pregnancy that has already begun. No opinion, no matter how passionate, can accurately contradict this fact: Emergency contraception is not an abortion, and cannot create an abortion.

There are now a dozen brands of emergency contraception available over the counter at drugstores and chains in virtually every city in America. With brand names like Plan B, My Choice, and Aftera, this product is a modern miracle, effective as much as 98 percent of the time if taken soon enough.

Why oh why oh why doesn’t every fertile, sexually active American have this product in their medicine chest? It’s inexpensive and lasts for five years; after that, celebrate that you didn’t need it, and replace it with a fresh package.

After 44 years as a sex therapist, very little surprises me. But I’m still amazed at the number of people who don’t use lube when they masturbate or have intercourse.

Some women are insulted when I suggest lube for intercourse. “I get plenty wet,” they protest indignantly. And when I suggest lube to men who have trouble entering a vagina, or whose erections are wobbly when they’re alone or with a partner, they respond as if I’ve accused them of being inept.

“Stop everything and reach for lube, right,” some patient will periodically sneer, as if I’m suggesting they reach for a diesel generator.

But we don’t use lube to solve a problem or address a failure. We use lube to make sex more enjoyable, with or without a partner. If you keep it handy where you usually have partner or solo sex, reaching for it can be simple and nonintrusive.

Lube is better than spit (which quickly disappears when absorbed), and better than olive oil or any other oil (which are difficult to get out of a vagina or anus when you’re done).

Every drugstore carries lube, typically near the condoms or tampons. Amazon carries 100 brands, which suggests just how common this product is. The easiest kind to use (and mandatory with condoms) are the water-soluble brands. A tip for condom users—put two drops inside the condom to increase heat transfer and make it stick to the penis better.

Pelvic floor therapy (PFPT) is a type of physical therapy that helps rehabilitate the muscles in the pelvic floor.

Women and men are typically referred to PFPT for painful sex or orgasm, postpartum issues, pelvic organ prolapse, hemorrhoids, and incontinence. In addition to treating chronically tight muscles, the therapist can teach exercises to strengthen and relax pelvic floor muscles.

PFPT is one of those treatment programs after which people say, “I feel so much better—and didn’t even realize how tight and sore I actually was until we fixed it.” If sex or orgasm hurt, or you have issues that your physician can’t explain or resolve, get a referral to one of these fabulous practitioners.

The more we know about estrogen replacement for middle-aged women, the better it looks.

And with 2,000,000 women entering menopause every year, the late 40s (a year or two before menopause often starts) is a special window when many women can use estrogen to protect themselves against health problems including dementia, heart disease, and osteoporosis.

But isn’t estrogen dangerous? Doesn’t it cause breast cancer? In a word, no.

That myth became widespread overnight in 2002 from methodological mistakes in a single report. Subsequent studies around the world have convincingly demolished this myth—but because “no actual problem” never gets the headlines that “wow—huge problem!” gets, millions of women and their doctors still believe that estrogen is dangerous. There’s also a role for testosterone supplements in women’s health.

The best books on this subject are Estrogen Matters by Bluming & Tavris and The Menopause Moment by Kelly Casperson. Each is fascinating, uplifting, and totally useful.

The sex therapy field was formalized by Masters & Johnson some 60 years ago. Usually offered by a psychologist or marriage and family therapist, sex therapy is sometimes offered by a nurse practitioner, social worker, or psychiatrist.

Sex therapists treat problems with erection, orgasm, and desire, as well as guilt, shame, anxiety, and curiosity. We also help individuals and couples think and talk about infidelity, nonmonogamy, kink, sexual orientation, pornography, and past trauma.

There are several thousand experienced sex therapists in the United States—at least a few in every medium and large city. And now with Zoom sessions, everyone can meet with a sex therapist if they want to.

So why don’t more people take advantage of these marvelous interventions?

So on Thanksgiving Day, give thanks that we in America have many sexual rights and access to many sex-related products. If appropriate, do consider pursuing one or more of them.

#4674. Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the company has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha showed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The new Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the company has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

#4673. The 10 Best Chinos for Men, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our editors found Lululemon and Bonobos to make some of the best.

I USED TO think chinos were the kind of pants your dad wore to a backyard barbecue in the early 2000s. You know—the stiff, boxy khaki pants sitting way too high on the waist that ended up looking like high-waters. But chinos have come a long way since then. These days, chinos look cleaner, fit better, and feel more comfortable than most denim I own. I can wear them to the office with a button-down, out to dinner with a blazer, or just throw them on with a tee and sneakers for a Yankees game.

Most of today’s styles now come with stretchy fabrics and moisture-wicking tech, and lightweight materials that make them way easier to wear year-round. Since 2020, the Men’s Health fashion team and I have tested more than 50 pairs—from slim-fit classics to more relaxed cuts—to find the chinos that belong in rotation. Without further ado, browse our selection with picks from Bonobos, Everlane, and Lululemon to find one that suits your style and elevates your everyday wardrobe.

After thoroughly putting Lululemon's ABC Pant to the test, I found that it flat-out outshines everything else in its class. The sweat-wicking, quick-drying, and wrinkle-resistant fabric with four-way stretch makes this pair feel like your favorite joggers disguised as office pants. Unlike the others on the list, it comes with their proprietary ABC (Anti-Ball Crushing) design. Our editors found it's basically a clever gusset that eases tension in the crotch and thigh area, so you never feel squeezed or restricted when you're walking or sitting for hours.

After owning this pair since 2020, its performance has never let us down once. The elastomultiester-polyester fabric blend makes it feel technical yet polished. It moves like activewear but looks structured enough for meeting or semi-dressy events. During brutal summer commutes, we stayed dry and comfortable, never dealing with that dreaded swampy feeling below deck.

The classic fit hits right in the middle, meaning not too slim, not too loose, and comes in a bunch of office-approved colors that look sharp from 9 to 5 and beyond. We've worn this pair everywhere: happy hours, long-haul flights, work dinners, the list goes on. Functionally, Lululemon thought of everything: hand pockets that don't bulge, a hidden zip pocket for your wallet, and even a side pocket to keep your phone secure while you're on the move.

Lululemon’s ABC pant is what guys wish their everyday slacks felt like—unrestrictive, clean as a whistle, and ridiculously comfortable.

Our testers all agreed that these are arguably the most comfortable chinos on the market. Once we slipped our legs into these pants, we found the overall fit and feel of the fabric to be 10/10. That’s not only because Bonobos offers five different fits to cater to your body type, but also because the brand infuses the cotton fabric with quite a bit of four-way stretch, making them extra versatile for days when you want to wear chino pants out to travel, commute, run errands, etc.

In our testing, we also found that the waistband felt comfortable because it curved to the shape of our hip. The fabric, after we wore them for hours on end, turned out to be moisture-wicking as well, and, all in all low-maintenance because it's wrinkle-resistant. And we love that Bonobos added a zip pocket to help us safely store our small stuff.

Dockers is known for pioneering the modern khaki and popularizing business-casual style. It’s no wonder the brand’s chinos are simply great pants, ticking off all the boxes: comfort, durability, low maintenance, and style that works for your day-to-day hustle. With a clean, flat front and a slightly tapered leg, they bring a relaxed vibe that works beyond the office. We can imagine how you might think they're only useful as a workwear staple, but make no mistake—they fit the bill for regular weekend outings, too. Whether paired with a T-shirt and sneakers or a polo and comfortable dress shoes, these chinos deliver every time.

What really sets the slim-fit trouser apart from others we’ve tested is the bi-stretch twill, a type of fabric that stretches both horizontally and vertically. During our experience, we found that guys with athletic legs can slip into these chinos without feeling squeezed. It was a breeze to simply put them on and go without having to waste time ironing.

Rhone's making an appearance twice on the list, and for good reason. The label makes another top-tier chino, designed with an innovative stretch aptly named Flex-Knit, which provides enough elastane to handle everything on your plate: eight-hour shifts, rounds of golf, long-haul flights, etc. In other words, you have maximum mobility to do it all and then some. The fabric is also wrinkle resistant, so no visible creases will throw you off your game.

To amp up our style, we matched these with a crisp Oxford shirt and some dapper lace-up loafers. Not to get things confused, this pant has a casual edge and can be dressed down with sneakers, too. We know there may be a bit of sticker shock when you glance at the price tag, but these chinos are durable enough to survive multiple wash cycles and still keep their fresh-off-the-rack look. Plus, this chino comes in a variety of fits: classic, slim, and skinny.

Visible creases in your pants can be a pain, cramping your style and throwing off that polished look you’re going for. That’s why we love Banana Republic’s wrinkle-resistant chinos. This pair is made with a high-stretch fabric that’s super smooth, sturdy, and won’t get in the way of things. Tailored to perfection, the mid-rise cut falls around the natural waistline and grants you the freedom to move as you wish.

During our testing, we found that it’s perfect for dressier occasions, but can easily be toned down for casual outings like an outdoor festival or weekend brunch. In terms of outfits, the chinos pair effortlessly with a crewneck sweater or henley tee for whatever’s on the agenda. The brand offers a range of colors, but if you opt for gray—you get a versatile, sleek option that goes with almost anything and adds a touch of sophistication to your appearance.

If you want a pair of chinos that are a little more tapered in the leg, Uniqlo’s slim-fit cut may be your best bet. In general, they’re made with close attention to detail. For one, the pants are enhanced with a cotton-spandex blend, which provides all-day-long softness and stretch without sacrificing a sharp style. While it’s not a traditional chino material, we found that it’s flexible enough to bend or squat. Also, the brand shied away from making the stitching visible for a streamlined look.

Having worn these pants to travel, we were impressed by how lightweight and smooth the fabric is. Despite the slim fit, the pants were not restricting in the least bit. In terms of color, there's a fair amount of neutrals that are easy to pair with your everyday wear. It's hard to go wrong with Uniqlo's chinos because they are suitable for any occasion—from work to meetings to date night to casual outings and everything in between.

Sometimes, chinos can feel a little stuffy but this relaxed fit keeps me cool and comfortable for hours. From my muggy subway commute to weaving through crowded city streets, I stay breezy and unbothered. The cotton fabric has this soft drape that doesn’t wrinkle, even after I’ve been sitting at my desk from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and by the time I’m heading to lunch or meeting a friend for happy hour after work, this chino still looks sharp.

The straight-leg cut falls on top of the shoe, without making me look like a slob. While it doesn’t come in multiple fits like Bonobos or Rhone options, you can pick from a few solid colors to rotate through the week. And yes, this pair comes with a higher price tag, but the quality speaks for itself: the material is thick enough to hold its shape yet breathable enough to keep me chill while running around photo shoot sets, crouching for shots, or darting between meetings. This chino also looks just as good outside the office for brunch or a museum trip. I’ve overstuffed the pockets a few times, but for a slim cardholder and some cash, they stay flat and clean.

Flint and Tinder’s pair stands out because it's designed as a hybrid between chinos and jeans, making it one of the most versatile pants out there. It's cut like a tailored chino but has the feel and flexibility of your favorite broken-in denim, thanks to its preshrunk cotton-stretch fabric blend. We found the midweight fabric works year-round—hence the "365" name—so you can wear them in any season. We've worn them during the winter and well into the spring, and they've held up through it all—whether layered with a heavy parka or paired with a breezy t-shirt when the temps start to rise.

This pair skews more into the casual workwear department, but you can sport them from the office to the bar with no problem at all. It's also garment-dyed for a lived-in look from day one and comes in several fits: classic, slim, straight, and tapered, to suit a bunch of different styles.

What's the next best thing close to slim-fit chino? Ding-ding-ding, skinny-fit. That is, one that's not constricting on your lower half. Before you jump ship, this pair from J.Crew isn't super tight like the skinny jeans that peaked in the early 2000s. For starters, it's infused with the brand's stretch technology that provides a subtle yet noticeable amount of give—to move every which way without feeling stiff and eliminate any annoying break-in period. Designed to sit below the waist, these pants are slim through the hip with a close-fitting leg, offering a more modern and streamlined silhouette.

Also, the structured twill-lined waistband with chambray binding adds a touch of durability and style, while the angled pockets offer easy access to your most valuable items. Let's not forget how versatile they are, too. This style works at the bar, the office, and even on the golf course. Our fashion editors recommend pairing this pant with a denim shacket layered over a white t-shirt for an easy, casual ensemble to hit the town.

Rhone totally gets it right with workout clothes, but the athleisure brand also has the everyday chinos down pat as well. This classic five-pocket style resembles your favorite jeans, but it’s super lightweight and way more comfortable than any stiff denim. We love that the fabric actually uses lyocell to amplify breathability and smoothness, which is comparable to the texture of silk. Our testers also found these chinos were able to wick away sweat and keep you dry during a busy day.

Designed for office professionals, the pants also boast a media pouch for your phone and a security zipper pocket for your cardholder. We keep them in rotation for the work week, but we can’t get enough of how sleek they look with a dress shirt for a weekend out on the town. The only qualm is that the waistband fades in comparison to others we’ve tried, in terms of stretch and flexibility.

When shopping for chinos or any other type of pants, the fabric choice is crucial, as it impacts comfort, durability, and overall appearance. Typically, chinos are made with a lightweight cotton blend to create a more comfortable wear for men. While many modern chinos incorporate stretch or performance fibers, traditional 100% cotton options are still widely available. Here’s a rundown of common fabrics and what they’re best for:

A classic choice for chinos due to its softness, breathability, and comfort. Cotton is ideal for casual wear and everyday use. It can be found in various weights and finishes, from lightweight and airy to heavier and more structured.

This is a type of weave rather than a fabric itself. Twill fabrics, often made from cotton, have a diagonal pattern that adds durability and a subtle texture.

Often used in blends, polyester adds durability and wrinkle resistance. It’s less breathable than cotton but can help chinos maintain their shape and resist stains. Polyester blends are ideal for a polished look with low maintenance.

Many chinos use fabric blends to combine the best properties of different materials. Common blends include cotton-polyester (for durability and wrinkle resistance) or cotton-spandex (for stretch and flexibility). Blends can provide a good balance of comfort, durability, and ease of care.

Fabrics with added spandex or elastane offer flexibility and comfort. These are great for chinos that need to accommodate a range of movements and provide a snug fit without losing their shape.

Chinos should fit comfortably around your waist and hips without being too tight or too loose. Look for options with a bit of stretch, as they often offer a better fit and more flexibility. When searching for the best chinos, you'll typically come across these main fits below.

A modern, tailored look that tapers slightly from the thigh down. The leg should taper slightly but not be so slim that it looks like skinny jeans. Great for guys who prefer a more streamlined silhouette without being too tight.

A classic, timeless cut that falls straight from the hips to the ankles. This fit works well for most body types and offers a more relaxed yet polished look.

Designed for guys with more muscular thighs, this fit offers extra room in the seat and thighs while still tapering toward the ankle. It gives a tailored look without feeling restrictive.

A roomier option with more space in the thigh and leg, ideal for casual wear or those who prioritize comfort over a tapered leg.

To find the best chinos, our fashion team, led by Style Director Christian Gollayan, focused on these key factors: style, fit, comfort, price point, versatility, and performance (including stretch, moisture-wicking, and breathability). We examined whether they fit true to size, whether the fabric could withstand hours of movement in different temperatures, and whether they could be worn for more than one occasion.

Our tested selection doesn't chase trends, rather it highlights chinos for men that fit great (even on athletic guys with bigger thighs), provide strong value and performance, and come in styles that'll still look sharp years from now. Keep reading to find out which pairs earned their stripes and landed a spot on our handpicked list.

When it comes to styling chinos for men, it's essential to strike the perfect balance between looking casual and looking polished. For starters, the safest way to style chinos is to opt for versatile colors like classic khaki, navy, or olive. Then, ensure your chinos have the right fit—a tailored fit, preferably, that accentuates your silhouette and is not too loose or tight. Then, for a smart-casual vibe, pair your chinos with crisp button-down shirts or polo shirts for your office days. For something a bit more laidback, dress down your chinos with a well-fitted t-shirt or sweater for your casual outings. For layering, chinos will match well with blazers and shackets for colder seasons. As for footwear, canvas sneakers and loafers in general will give your chinos a more casual feel, while leather sneakers and dress shoes are perfect for dressing up chinos for a more put-together look. We also encourage wearing chinos with a leather belt.

If you're a fit guy looking for chinos that'll match your athletic build, we have some recommendations. Typically, guys who have larger legs will find that off-the-rack chinos are loose around the waist. Bodybuilders tend to run into this problem where they have to size up to get normal chinos to fit their quads, but since they have a slighter waist, it’s often loose. For maximum comfort, look for pants with more room in the quads and glutes while tapering up the waist for an athletic fit.

In short, chinos are a style of trousers, whereas khaki mainly refers to a light brown or tan color. Specifically, chinos are pants typically made of cotton twill fabric, which is durable, light, and breathable, and come in a variety of colors beyond the traditional khaki. Khakis often mean pants made in khaki colors and the term is now often used to describe casual cotton trousers often in a beige or tan color.

While khakis share similarities with chinos, the term is sometimes used more narrowly to refer specifically to beige or tan-colored casual pants, whereas chinos specifically refer to a pants style made in a certain fabric and design.

So all khakis can be chinos, but not all chinos are necessarily khakis since chinos can come in every color imaginable.

Modern chinos are often made with cotton blends that incorporate a little stretch for added flexibility and comfort. Performance-oriented versions may also use fabrics like polyester or nylon to add features such as moisture-wicking, breathability, or quick-drying properties. Traditional 100% cotton chinos are still widely available, too.

You bet your ass we do! Chinos remain a wardrobe staple in men's fashion because they’re so versatile, comfortable, and stylish for different occasions. They can be dressed up or down for a casual day out, a semi-formal event, or even an office day in the workplace. Since chinos are often made of soft, breathable, and light fabric, they can transition from warm summers to cooler days. Men’s chinos are also popular because they are super easy to style—whether it’s for your workplace attire or your weekend wear, they will find a way to be part of your fit. Lastly, chino pants just have that classic, clean, enduring appeal, making them the go-to pants style for many men.

#4672. How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 8:49 AM EST

Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

But these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” says Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

“You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” says Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) plan to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley says the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into new materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

#4671. The 10 Best Fitness Trackers for Women, Tested and Reviewed by Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals. You may want a smartwatch that can handle calls and texts along with fitness data tracking, or maybe you’re looking for a distraction-free screenless band that quietly tracks your metrics in the background. If running is your thing, you may want a smartwatch with GPS accuracy and real-time training metrics that are easy to read during a run, and if you’re focused on improving sleep, you may prefer a smart ring that won’t feel bulky overnight.

For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.

Whoop earned the top spot for the best overall fitness tracker because it provides deeper understanding of your data while also giving context of what all that data means. I’ve been using a Whoop for the past several years, and of all the fitness tracker options I’ve tested, it remains my hands-down favorite. It delivers some of the most useful recovery, sleep, and strain insights in a distraction-free design that’s so comfortable I often completely forget that I’m wearing it. The battery life is impressive, and I only have to charge mine twice a month.

Whoop 5.0 is built on the foundation of an app that offers analysis of your metrics paired with context, so you actually learn what all the numbers mean for your health and training. The screen-free design means that instead of buzzing constantly or encouraging you to check another display, it quietly tracks your metrics in the background and turns that data into recovery, strain, sleep data to give you an overall picture of your fitness within an app.

The sensor platform uses multi-wavelength optical heart rate sensors, skin-temperature sensing, blood oxygen monitoring, and accelerometer and gyroscope motion sensors to collect data continuously, tracking your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, strain, and recovery.

The app then interprets those numbers, in a way that feels more actionable than raw data alone, to generate a daily readiness score that indicates how much physical exertion your body is up for on any given day (00033though it’s always important to listen to your body regardless of what a wearable says). If you wake up with a low recovery score, for example, Whoop may recommend reducing workout intensity. If your sleep debt is climbing, it will show how much rest you need to get back on track.

It also offers other behavior change suggestions that could improve how you feel based on the data it collects about you and your habits over time. In fact, the in-depth habit tracking feature offers some of the most valuable insights into how day-to-day behaviors affect us physiologically. As a trainer, this has been one of the features I've seen make the most long-term impact with clients, as it really helps them connect the dots and understand how everything is interrelated.

Whoop 5.0 does require a membership and there are three different tiers, the main difference being the level of insights and analysis. Whoop One covers the core Whoop experience, including sleep, strain, recovery, steps, activity monitoring, heart-rate tracking, and women’s hormonal insights, which helps us see how menstrual cycle phases may relate to sleep, recovery, and performance. Whoop Peak adds a broader health and wellness layer, including health monitor, stress monitor, healthspan, and more advanced coaching-style insights for users who want to connect daily habits with longer-term performance and recovery trends (this is the tier I personally go with). Whoop Life is the most advanced tier, adding heart-health features such as ECG, irregular heart rhythm notifications, and blood pressure insights where available. Ultimately, the difference between the tiers is less about the tracker experience itself and more about how much interpretation, health context, and advanced monitoring you want.

The tradeoff is cost. Since Whoop uses a membership model, it will end up being more expensive over time than a tracker that doesn’t require a subscription. It also is not the best choice if you want live pace, distance, or workout stats on your wrist during a run. For that, a Garmin, Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, or COROS watch will be more practical.

The Google Fitbit Inspire earned its spot as the best budget pick because it gives you the core fitness-tracking features most people want in a slim and approachable design. It’s not trying to be a full smartwatch or a performance running watch. Instead, it focuses on the basics: steps, heart rate, workouts, sleep, active minutes, and general wellness trends.

That simplicity makes the Fitbit Inspire a good entry point for someone who wants to become more aware of their fitness data without getting buried in advanced metrics. It can track walks, gym workouts, casual runs, and sleep, while the Fitbit app makes the data easy to understand. You can quickly see how much movement you got throughout the day, how long you slept, and how your habits are trending over time. Additionally, you’ll get a stress management score, guided breathing sessions, and reminders to move.

It is also one of the easiest trackers to wear all day. The band is slim enough to feel less bulky than a smartwatch, and the display is small but still easy to use for checking basic stats. If your main goals are walking more, staying accountable, improving sleep habits, or getting started with activity tracking, the Inspire offers strong value.

The main limitation is that it’s not necessarily built for serious training. Depending on the model, the GPS may rely on your phone rather than being fully built into the device, and runners who want advanced pace analysis, training load, recovery guidance, or race tools will likely outgrow it. But for the price, it’s one of the most practical fitness trackers for everyday use.

The Apple Watch Series 12 blends health tracking, workout features, smartwatch convenience, and safety tools better than almost any other wearable. If you already use an iPhone, this is the most seamless option in our guide.

The Series 12 features more advanced sensor capabilities, including an upgraded optical heart sensor that measures heart rate every five seconds, and tracks HRV more frequently. WH associate fitness editor Addison Aloin wrote in her review that the Series 12 has “a great baseline of health and fitness features.”

The Series 12 tracks a wide range of workouts, including running, walking, cycling, strength training, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, swimming, hiking, and many more. During activity, the display is bright and you can easily view data like pace, distance, heart rate, time, and workout zones during runs and workouts. It also integrates smoothly with Apple Fitness+, the Health app, and third-party training apps.

One of the most meaningful updates the Series 12 got is a new readiness score, which uses recent activity, training load, your sleep score, and overnight metrics like heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and recovery HRV to estimate how prepared your body is for exertion. The score runs from 0 to 10 and gives you a recommendation for your day, such as Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. “My only complaint is that it’s kind of hard to find the readiness score on the watch and in the Health app,” Aloin says.

Since it’s so much more than just a tracker you wear during workout, the Apple Watch also offers a lot of versatility. It can handle notifications, calls, music, maps, timers, contactless payments, fall detection, and emergency features, making it a strong option for anyone who wants one device that can move between workouts and everyday life.

It is also a good pick for people who like motivational nudges. Apple’s activity rings are simple, visual, and surprisingly effective if you respond well to daily goals. If you want coaching-style feedback without digging through complex training dashboards, the Series 12’s newer software can translate health and fitness data into easily digestible prompts.

The Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, and Apple says 15 minutes of charging can add up to 12 hours of battery. That makes it more manageable for overnight sleep tracking, but it still requires more planning than fitness trackers that last several days or longer on a single charge. “I’ve found the battery life is awesome for everyday use, but usually does need a charge every other day or so,” Aloin says.

Read More: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4

The Google Fitbit Air gives you the quiet, distraction-free experience of a screenless wearable at a more approachable price point than premium recovery bands. The Fitbit Air tracks core metrics like activity, heart rate, sleep, and wellness trends over time, then sends that information to your phone.

Since there’s no screen, you’re not checking your wrist throughout the day. That makes it a strong option for anyone who wants to be more mindful about movement and sleep but doesn’t want a smartwatch. It’s also a good fit for people who are curious about screenless tracking but are not ready to commit to a more expensive platform. It offers a simpler, lower-pressure way to see whether passive health tracking actually helps your routine.

The Fitbit app is another advantage. Fitbit’s platform is approachable, especially for beginners, and tends to present health data in a way that feels less intimidating than more athlete-focused apps. That makes the Air a strong choice for casual users who want guidance without performance overload.

The main limitation is that a screenless budget tracker will not replace a running watch or smartwatch. You will not get the same real-time workout stats, app support, phone features, or advanced training analysis. But if you want affordable, low-distraction tracking, Fitbit Air is a compelling pick.

The Coros Pace 4 is our best lightweight pick because it delivers serious training features in a watch that feels easy to wear. After testing the watch for two months, MH deputy features editor Carina Hsieh said that it feels so lightweight that you forget it’s there. It’s especially appealing for runners and fitness-minded users who want more data than a basic tracker can provide but don’t want a bulky smartwatch.

Coros has built a strong reputation among runners because its watches tend to offer excellent battery life, practical training tools, and reliable GPS. The Pace 4 continues that tradition. “I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive and quick the GPS signal was on runs,” Hsieh said. She also noted that the watch had an exceptionally long battery life during her testing, and that she only had to charge it twice in two months.

For runners, the Pace 4 can track pace, distance, heart rate, route data, workouts, recovery, and training trends. Features like race predictions, virtual pacing, breadcrumb navigation, and personalized training tools make it feel like a strong contender for anyone who is a serious runner. It is also useful for people who cross-train, since it can handle gym workouts, cycling, walking, and other activities.

A big reason to choose the Pace 4 over other smartwatches is that it feels purpose-built for fitness. You’re not paying for a huge app ecosystem or phone-like features. Instead, you’re getting a lightweight training watch that can help you understand your fitness, recovery, and progress.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is the best fitness tracker for Android users, especially anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone. It offers a polished smartwatch experience with robust health and fitness tools, making it a bit like an Android equivalent to the Apple Watch. WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders, who has tested multiple wearables over the years, says she usually struggles to wear trackers consistently because the bands were uncomfortable overnight. But the Galaxy Watch 9 changed that. “The band is surprisingly comfortable to wear and, dare I say, actually looks good,” she said.

This smartwatch tracks everyday activity, steps, heart rate, workouts, stress, sleep, and recovery-style metrics. It also includes Samsung’s Vitals feature, which monitors overnight patterns including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and other sleep-related signals, then compares them against your personal baseline. Saunders says it took about a full week for her baseline to set up, and anything outside of her normal range appeared in orange in the app, making it easy to compare metrics and spot subtle changes over time.

It also tracks a wide range of exercise modes, and its running features are useful for people who want coaching-style tools. Samsung’s body composition measurement feature can also be helpful for observing trends over time, though the numbers should be treated as estimates rather than medical-grade measurements. Saunders also liked the sleep features, including sleep quality tracking and snore detection, which she found both funny and potentially useful for better understanding nighttime habits.

The watch pairs easily with Galaxy phones, and the Samsung Health app organizes fitness and wellness data in an approachable way. If you want a tracker that can monitor workouts in the morning, handle notifications during the day, and track sleep at night, the Galaxy Watch 9 is a strong choice. In her testing, Saunders found it to be stylish and effective, adding that it would make a great gift for someone starting a health journey or looking for more detailed insights.

The Oura Ring 5 offers robust health and sleep tracking in the most discreet package of all the fitness trackers in this guide. If you don’t like wearing a watch around the clock or simply prefer jewelry over a wristband, Oura is the easiest fitness tracker to live with. In her review, WH associate editor Olivia Luppino said it’s the only fitness tracker she’s ever used that she hasn’t wanted to take off.

The Oura Ring’s biggest strength is passive health tracking. It’s designed to unobtrusively monitor your body in the background, and then translate that information into readiness, sleep, activity, stress, temperature, and recovery insights in an easy to use app. It can be especially helpful for people who want to understand how sleep, illness, stress, menstrual cycle changes, and daily habits affect energy.

For sleep tracking, the Ring 5 is one of the more comfortable options since a ring is less bulky than a watch, and many people find it easier to wear overnight. The app also makes sleep data easy to understand, showing not just how long you slept but how restorative that sleep may have been.

The tradeoff is workout tracking. Oura can track activity and has improved its fitness features, but it’s still not the best choice for people who want real-time stats during runs, strength workouts, or cycling sessions. It can also interfere with grip during weightlifting and kettlebell training. If you want to glance at pace, heart rate, or intervals mid-workout, choose a watch. If you want discreet, all-day and all-night health tracking, choose a smart ring.

For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 570 sits in a sweet spot between advanced training watches and an everyday wearable. Garmin makes several excellent Forerunner models, but the 570 offers a mix of running metrics, GPS tools, recovery insights, smartwatch features, and comfortable wearability for runners who want more than the basics without jumping straight to flagship option.

The Forerunner 570 is designed to be useful for structured training with its capability to track runs, intervals, long runs, tempo sessions, races, recovery runs, and cross-training workouts. It also gives runners access to Garmin’s broader training ecosystem, including performance metrics, suggested workouts, recovery guidance, HRV status, sleep data, training readiness-style insights, and race-related tools. For someone training for a 5K, half marathon, marathon, or simply trying to become a more consistent runner, those features can be super useful.

It has a bright AMOLED display, touchscreen support as well as physical buttons, a feature that’s especially notable for runners since touchscreens can sometimes be frustrating with sweat, rain, or gloves. Battery life varies from 8 hours to up to 10 days depending on how many features you’re using.

The biggest drawback is price. Though it’s not the priciest Forerunner offering out there, the Forerunner 570 is not inexpensive, and newer runners who only want pace, distance, and heart rate may be perfectly happy with a more affordable Forerunner model. But runners who want a capable watch they won’t outgrow, the 570 is a great option.

The Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless tracker for lovers of the Garmin fitness ecosystem, since it integrates seamlessly with Garmin’s other tech. It delivers health and activity tracking without adding another display to your life, and is especially well suited for anyone who wants to use Garmin Connect but doesn't want to wear a full Garmin watch all day long.

That makes Cirqa especially useful for athletes who already own a Garmin running, cycling, or outdoor watch. You may want to wear your Forerunner for workouts and during runs, but prefer something smaller and screen-free for sleep, recovery, or everyday tracking. The Cirqa fills that gap.

It also has a cost advantage over some screenless competitors because it doesn’t require a subscription. That makes it appealing for Garmin loyalists who want ongoing tracking without committing to a monthly membership.

The Cirqa isn’t the best choice if you want live workout stats, on-wrist coaching, or a display for pace and distance, and a Garmin watch would be better for that. But as a low-distraction daily tracker that complements Garmin’s training platform, Cirqa is a welcome addition to the category.

The Google Fitbit Edge bridges the gap between a simple Fitbit band and a full smartwatch, making it a strong choice if you want a display but don’t want a bulkier smartwatch. It gives you a screen for checking stats, starting workouts, reviewing progress, and seeing basic information at a glance.

Compared with the Fitbit Air, the Edge is more interactive, compared with the Inspire, it’s a more advanced option, and compared with a Pixel Watch, it’s simpler to use and more fitness focused. It offers enough features to be useful throughout the day, tracking activity, workouts, sleep, heart-rate trends, and daily wellness data, while still keeping the overall experience lighter than a smartwatch. If you want a compact Google Fitbit tracker with a screen and stronger features than the entry-level models, the Edge is the best fit.

A good heart rate monitor is one of the most important features to look for in a fitness tracker, whether you’re training seriously or just getting started. Heart rate data can help you better understand exercise intensity, track effort during workouts, and monitor resting heart rate over time, which can be a useful marker of cardiovascular fitness. While wrist-based trackers typically aren’t as precise as chest straps, they can still offer a helpful read on exertion levels during moderate to intense activity, according to a 2019 study in Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy.

Sleep tracking can be a useful feature because sleep plays a major role in recovery, energy, mood, and overall performance. By tracking patterns like sleep duration, consistency, and overnight restlessness, a fitness tracker can help you spot habits that may be affecting how you feel the next day. Many models also break down sleep stages, show trends over time, and offer recovery or readiness insights based on your nightly data. While the numbers aren’t always perfect, they can provide a helpful starting point for understanding your routine and making small changes, like adjusting bedtime, limiting late caffeine, or improving sleep consistency.

Weight may not seem that important at first, but it matters when you’re wearing a fitness tracker all day and night. A larger, heavier model can feel more noticeable over time, especially during sleep or long workouts. There’s no single ideal size, and the best option will depend on how you plan to use it.

If you run, hike, or spend a lot of time outdoors, it may be worth choosing a more durable model, even if it’s slightly bulkier. For everyday wear, walking, strength training, or mostly indoor workouts, a lighter, lower-profile tracker may be more comfortable. Ultimately, the right fit comes down to your activity level, wrist size, and what you’ll actually want to keep wearing.

Many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Whoop 5.0. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that an option like the Apple Watch Series 12 needs to be charged every day and it’s still one of our absolute favorites. Ultimately it comes down to how a trackers charging needs will fit into your routine.

As with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that’s easy to use. If your new tracker isn’t intuitive for you to set up or use daily, you’re far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's why it’s smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.

I’ve been a certified personal trainer for more than a decade, and together with other Women’s Health editors, I’m constantly testing the latest fitness trackers across key factors like durability, comfort, features, and accuracy. We tested them during our workouts, on our runs, in Pilates class, and more. And of course, we tested them during sleep. Whether you’re training regularly or just want something for everyday activity tracking, the models we tested for the latest update range from basic fitness trackers to powerful smartwatches and everything in between.

#4670. Hyundai is overhauling the Kona, and it looks like it may still be offered as an EV after all

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai said the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car)

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

While earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

The updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the new Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

#4669. Mindfulness, Motivational Interviewing, and Exposure in IFS

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Here’s a question in the holiday spirit: What do you get by mixing a nonalcoholic goblet of mindfulness (let’s say, mint water), a mug of motivational interviewing (lemon water), and a glass of exposure therapy (spring water)? My answer: an elixir called Internal Family Systems (IFS), an approach to therapy and life that's based on two big assumptions, each with important subcategories.

First, the mind is plural; we all have parts, and when one part gets hurt and banished from consciousness, other (often slightly older) parts come online to protect it. The first protectors, the proactive ones, take on the job of inhibiting genuine self-expression. Some warn the hurt part (called an exile in IFS), some criticize, and some perform socially—all with the aim of preventing more harm. As their inhibitions and shaming grow intense, a set of reactive protectors come online to offer relief with various disinhibitions and addictive processes that are highly effective at distracting from or soothing emotional pain in the short run.

While their radically different tactics naturally put them in conflict, both sides unintentionally aggravate the underlying emotional pain of exiled parts. When proactive protectors shame exiles, they feel even worse; when they feel worse, reactive protectors feel obliged to launch some kind of disinhibition, often in the form of an addictive process. In turn, disinhibitions inspire more shaming, and so matters escalate.

But this is not the end of the story. The second assumption made in IFS is that the mind has the capacity to receive (or produce, depending on your beliefs) a consciousness that is qualitatively different from parts. This different consciousness, called Self in IFS, is characterized by inviting mental states like curiosity, kindness, connectedness, clarity, courage, and compassion. Parts need, and indeed thrive under, the influence and guidance of Self. From the IFS perspective, we suffer when our parts are cut off from Self and revive when that connection heals.

The first step in IFS therapy is to engage protectors. Their willingness is an essential element of therapy for any client, even those who are mandated. That said, the IFS way of encouraging protectors to be willing to engage is paradoxical. After calling the client’s attention to their internal experience, we ask them to look around for unwillingness. For example, if a client comes to therapy eager to change a habit like drinking a lot at the end of the day, the therapist asks if any other part either doesn’t believe change is possible or has reason to hold onto the status quo. Eventually, respect and inclusion—all parts are welcome—encourage even the most reluctant protectors to engage.

While IFS treatment comes in unequal portions, one for protectors and the other for exiles, we invite attention and willingness (those ingredients of mindfulness) throughout. But what about the mug of motivational interviewing? This tart aperitif is for protectors: What do you do? What would happen if you stopped doing it? Who do you protect? Are you tired of all this responsibility? Are your tactics working? Are you willing to try something new? Are you willing to meet someone else inside who can help? Let’s call it multi-player motivational interviewing. It goes on until protectors are willing to allow the Self to have contact with an exile.

We can only proceed to exposure in the second portion of IFS therapy (which ironically often takes far less time) when protectors say yes, and they will only say yes when everyone feels sufficiently connected to Self. In this second portion of therapy, exiles revisit those moments when the worst possible news landed (I’m weak, I’m alone, I’m worthless). These are the conclusions protectors have always feared. Keep in mind that even as exiles stayed desperately hopeful, protectors have desperately feared their hope. For protectors, it’s axiomatic that reliving terrible moments will be excruciating, pointless, and possibly dangerous. While protectors always feel responsible for the system’s survival, they’ve never succeeded in challenging identity insults that took root in vulnerability.

Our job is to persuade them to risk finding out if Self has the power to falsify identity insults. While we can explain that Self is the guardian who will take care of everyone going forward and that Self can even rescue parts who are trapped in the past, we’re asking them to try something new, and it feels risky. We can’t force them. They have to be willing.

We can, however, promise that it won’t be a careless exercise. When the exile tells its story, other parts will not hear—and we’re not expecting them to learn to tolerate—a tale of defeat and humiliation. Accompanied by Self, in an environment of validation, the exile will have the opportunity to revise its bad experiences in real time and come to a new conclusion: I’m legitimate, my feelings are valid, I’m not alone. A bad thing happened to me, but I’m not bad.

IFS calls this witnessing. We can also call it exposure. As many IFS practitioners have written, the compassion and hand-holding of the IFS brand of exposure is tailor-made to calm uncertainty and falsify negative identity beliefs.

While IFS therapy is accumulating an evidence base, I keep in mind what it shares with various thoroughly researched mental health treatments, not least mindfulness, motivational interviewing, and exposure.

#4668. F1 Driver Isack Hadjar Has a Very Specific 9-Minute Rule

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The 22-year-old Red Bull racer on his pre-race routine, the workout he hates, and his latest obsession: GTA IV.

ISACK HADJAR HAS a problem. The 22-year-old Red Bull Formula 1 driver has finally gotten his hands on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he's slightly concerned about what that might do to his free time.

“It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. He's only managed to squeeze in about 25 minutes of gameplay so far this weekend, but his verdict is already in: “It's amazing.”

For now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight. “I'm a professional,” he says with a smirk. “When I know it's time to go to sleep, I go to sleep.”

That level of discipline extends well beyond bedtime. In a sport that demands lightning-fast reflexes, intense concentration, and serious physical endurance, Hadjar has developed a pretty specific routine to get his brain and body ready to perform.

Take his pre-race ritual, which he has down to a science. He stretches and warms up with his trainer, including juggling and reaction-time tests to prime the brain. He listens to rap music—French, American, or British—to get himself hyped.

Then, exactly nine minutes before the race begins, he starts putting in his earpieces. “Not 10, not 11, nine," he says.

It's not a superstition or a lucky number. (That would be six, the number he drives with for Red Bull.) It’s simply what he’s found to be the perfect amount of time to get in the car and get ready to race. “I hate staying in the car doing nothing,” he says. “So for me, nine minutes is the maximum time.”

While he enjoys the pre-race preparation, there's one part of training he'd happily skip: zone 2 cardio, running at a moderate pace to power up his endurance.

“It’s just boring. I like conditioning more,” he says. To get through it, he puts on a movie, TV show, or music. “It goes by quickly in the end, but it's just, I feel like it's a waste of time. But it's very important.”

When the race is over, Hadjar's routine is considerably more relaxed. A good meal helps him switch his brain off—specifically, a burger with caramelized onions, cheddar, tomato, and lettuce. He’ll also watch anime and FaceTime his parents, especially after a good result.

And now, of course, there will be GTA VI waiting for him. Whether he'll be able to stick to that bedtime routine is another question.

Catch Hadjar in action this weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, streaming live (and for free!) on Apple TV.

#4667. 9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 11:06 AM EST

The Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

They were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially important, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.
